newsitem.title: GERMANY: German markets lose as Krupp backs down.
newsitem.headline: German markets lose as Krupp backs down.

text.p: Germany's politicians and labour unions may be happy with the withdrawal of steel group Krupp's hostile bid for Thyssen AG, but industry analysts said on Tuesday it could turn out to be a blow for German financial markets.

The decision by Gerhard Cromme, the brash chairman of Fried. Krupp AG Hoesch Krupp, to withdraw his bid for all of Thyssen and settle for a merger of their two steel companies is seen as a victory for German consensus-style politics.

But it is just this resistance against allowing market forces to sort out the winners and losers, and the repeated intervention of politicians into business matters, that has kept foreign investors wary of German equities.
"This is another manifestation of the provincial nature of Germany's capital markets," said Horst Frey, analyst with ABN Amro.

"Instead of demonstrating a functioning market-based system, in which it is possible to respond to a lack of management activity with a take-over attempt, the international community is laughing about this farce," he said.

Monday's withdrawal has highlighted the difference between the German preference for consensus, on which the post-war economic miracle was based, and the more aggressive market-led approach of the "Anglo-Saxon" economies, notably the United States and Britain.
Unions and many politicians opposed the hostile bid as it was likely to result in heavy job losses at a time when German unemployment is already the highest since 1933.
Paribas Capital Markets said in a report that Krupp's failed bid showed Germany was "not ready for Anglo-Saxon style activities which enhance shareholder value and streamline businesses".

Paribas likened Krupp's defeat to a recent decision by pharamceuticals and chemicals group Hoechst AG to drop plans to list its Hoechst Marion Roussel unit, which disappointed international investors.
"Overall, these two news items make the German stock market less attractive than it appeared as much of the reason for buying the market was the hope that German management could improve," it said.

Cromme shocked Germany's political establishment last week when he launched a rare hostile takeover of bigger rival Thyssen, bidding 435 marks ($258) a share, which amounted to a 25 percent premium on the company's share price at the time.

The bid drove up the share prices of both companies. But the disappointment over Krupp's decision on Monday to withdraw its bid and settle for closer co-operation with Thyssen caused shares to tumble in Tuesday trade.
Shares in Thyssen ended bourse trade down 10.06 percent at 375.50 marks, while the overall DAX index ended trade at 3,349.14 points, up 27.30 points or 0.82 percent.
Krupp-Hoesch shares also ended the day lower, down 7.50 marks or 2.22 percent at 331 marks.

After Cromme launched the bid, German politicians from the state government of North Rhine-Westphalia -- where the steel industry is based -- to Chancellor Helmut Kohl appealed to the companies to bear the 4.7 million jobless in mind.

Some politicians pointed the finger at Cromme and Deutsche Bank AG, Germany's biggest bank that is seen as the main financier of the takeover, saying the takeover attempt was another step that would lead to the "Americanisation" of German society.
Friedhelm Ost, a member of Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) and head of parliament's economic affairs committee, said he now hoped the two companies would move from hostility towards co-operation.
He praised Deutsche Bank's bail-out of companies such as Metallgesellschaft and Kloeckner-Humboldt-Deutz, but added that he wished the banks exercised "more social sensitivity".
The opposition Social Democrats (SPD) took the opportunity to call for greater control of German banks.

Ingrid Mattheus-Maier, SPD finance expert, urged the government to present legislation to limit banks' holdings in companies to five percent, block banks from serving as proxies for shareholders at annual meetings and limit the number of board seats that bank executives may hold.
($ = 1.686 German Marks)
